newsitem.title: FINLAND: LIPPONEN AT SAK MEET NEARLY SILENT ON BUFFER FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: LIPPONEN AT SAK MEET NEARLY SILENT ON BUFFER FUNDS.

text.p: Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on Friday spoke in cautious terms about the possibility of buffer funds aimed at cushioning the impact of cyclical downturns on corporate profits and employment if Finland joined EMU.

Speaking at the council meeting of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK), Finland's biggest trade union group, Lipponen said the costs of contributions to all kinds of funds should be in line with overall economic policy.
SAK chairman Lauri Ihalainen opened the council meeting by calling for tripartite talks between unions, employers and the government on nationwide buffer funds, which employers oppose.

"The government is ready to continue with tripartite cooperation also in preparing for EMU in the spirit that the economy and the labour markets must be developed towards stable economic conditions regardless of whether we join EMU among the first (countries) or not," Lipponen said.
"Among funds, the state budget is the most important one and it should be brought gradually into surplus," he said.
"The strengthening of corporate capital structures plays its own important role. Developing the wage formation system is a third central avenue of action," he added.

"In talks between the labour market organisations and, where appropriate, in tripartite talks, there will hopefully be results on the decisions needed on employee funds and funds for training," Lipponen said, but did not elaborate.
Keeping the work pension fund (TEL) system in good shape was among Finland's strengths in an EMU environment, he added.

"The funds must be funded, which means taxation or contributions paid by taxpayers, employers or wage earners. The costs of this must be adapted so that they are in line with overall economic policy," Lipponen said, but gave no details.
He said, however, that EU member countries were hardly likely to accept higher contributions to any scheme.
"Cohesion funds should be used ever more for employment and that area emphasised more than the expensive and status quo agriculture policy," Lipponen said.
